GS Paper III · Economy · Chapter 1 of 8

State of the Economy: Pushing the Growth FrontierPriority: see PYQ box

Handout pp 4-20Handwritten format · mnemonics and PYQs at each topicPYQ lens: 2017, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2024
PYQ LENS: 5 questions in your PYQ file touch this chapter (2017 · 2019 · 2020 · 2021 · 2024)Hot spots: potential GDP, "steady growth + low inflation = good shape?", GDP / CPI methodology change
THIS CHAPTER IN 60 SECONDS
  • World: growth is soft and prices are sticky; the USA grows on AI investment, Europe is mixed, China is deflating, Japan's carry trade has lost charm. Countries now use trade, tech and money as weapons (economic statecraft).
  • India FY26: real GDP growth 7.4%, fastest among major economies for the 4th year. Consumption is 61% of GDP, investment (GFCF) 30%, exports 21.5%.
  • Supply side: industry (manufacturing 8.4%) and services (9.1%) lead; agriculture is a stabiliser (GVA 3.6%, below its 4.5% average).
  • Prices and money: headline CPI fell to 1.7%; repo rate cut by 125 bps; gross NPA at a multi-decade low of 2.2%; fiscal deficit target 4.4% of GDP.
  • Data: India is rebasing GDP, IIP, WPI (2022-23) and CPI (2024), adding new surveys, and moving from WPI to PPI.
  • Outlook: medium-term potential growth near 7%, but five frictions remain (slow nominal growth, jobs mismatch, shy private capex, external pressure, strategic gap).
Understand it firstThink of the economy as a car on a long road. The world is the weather (storms, tariffs, fragmentation). FY26 numbers show the car is running fast and cool (7.4% growth, 1.7% inflation). Statistics reform is replacing the old dashboard so the driver reads speed correctly. Medium-term potential asks: how fast can the car keep running without overheating? This picture is a memory aid, not from the handout.
WORDS YOU NEED FIRST
WordPlain meaning (aid: verify before quoting)
Economic statecraftDeliberate use of economic means (trade, money, technology) to reach strategic goals. The handout's own definition.
Friendshoring / nearshoringMoving supply chains to friendly or nearby countries instead of the cheapest one.
FAE / H1 / FY26FAE = First Advance Estimate; H1 = first half of the year (April to September); FY26 = financial year 2025-26.
PFCE · GFCE · GFCFPrivate consumption spending · government consumption spending · gross fixed capital formation (investment). Together with exports they are the demand side of GDP.
GVAGross Value Added: output minus inputs, by sector. The supply side of GDP.
Base yearThe year whose prices and weights a statistical index uses as its "100". Old base years drift away from today's economy.
NowcastingEstimating the current quarter's GDP growth before official data comes, from high-frequency indicators.
Potential growthThe medium-term growth rate the economy can sustain, driven by capital stock, labour input and trend TFP (the handout's three drivers).
RememberOne line to carry: India is growing fast with low inflation and strong fiscal credibility, but the world is weaponising interdependence, so the goal is resilience plus strategic indispensability, measured with modern data.
RememberPrelims hook: 7.4% · 61.5/9.9/30.0/21.5 · CPI 1.7% · repo -125 bps · GNPA 2.2% · base years (2022-23, CPI 2024) · 299 → 358 CPI items · WPI 697 → 957 items. Mains hook: "good shape or not?" (2019), potential GDP (2020), GDP methodology (2021): write strengths → frictions → way forward.

Short forms in the opening block

AI = Artificial Intelligence (computer systems that do tasks needing human-like learning or judgement)

CPI = Consumer Price Index (measures retail inflation from a basket of goods and services households buy)

FAE = First Advance Estimate (first official estimate of annual GDP, made before the year ends)

FDI = Foreign Direct Investment (long-term investment by a foreign firm in a business in another country)

FY26 = Financial Year 2025-26 (April 2025 to March 2026)

GDP = Gross Domestic Product (value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year)

GFCE = Government Final Consumption Expenditure (government spending on its own consumption; part of GDP)

GFCF = Gross Fixed Capital Formation (investment in assets like machinery, buildings and infrastructure; the investment part of GDP)

GNPA = Gross Non-Performing Assets (total bad loans of banks as a share of loans (the handout gives 2.2%))

GVA = Gross Value Added (value of output minus inputs, by sector; the supply side of GDP)

IIP = Index of Industrial Production (monthly index of output in mining, manufacturing and electricity)

NPA = Non-Performing Asset (a bank loan that has stopped being repaid)

PFCE = Private Final Consumption Expenditure (household spending; the consumption part of GDP)

PPI = Producer Price Index (index of prices producers receive for goods and services; replaces WPI)

TFP = Total Factor Productivity (output growth not explained by more capital or labour: efficiency and technology)

USA = United States of America (one of the countries the handout names for school-level vocational exposure)

WPI = Wholesale Price Index (index of goods prices at the wholesale stage; being phased out for PPI)

Resurgence of economic statecraft
Understand it firstIf two shopkeepers depend on each other, both are safer. But if one can stop supplying the other, the dependence becomes a weapon. That is economic statecraft: interdependence is both a source of stability and a channel of vulnerability (the teacher's own arrow chain).
NoteDefinition (board p.5): deliberate use of economic means to achieve strategic ends.
Four drivers (from the infographic on p.5)
#DriverWhat it means (as printed)
1Inward-looking prioritiesResurgence of ultra-nationalism and an anti-immigrant stance, hardening domestic borders and constraining labour mobility.
2Countries sceptical of free trade and multilateral institutionsLarge and concentrated global trade imbalances (large surplus nations vs large deficit nations).
3Surplus and deficit nations diverge in the pace of creation and absorptionFast creation vs slow absorption stress and fracture the global economic landscape.
4Lack of updated global normsFragmented and polarised global order, and institutional and financial weakening of international standard-setting bodies.
NoteThe infographic's base line: these drivers reinforce each other, enabling states to weaponise interdependence, manage vulnerabilities and pursue power in an uncertain, competitive global environment.
MNEMONICSLIDFour drivers, order does not matter, so rearranged: Sceptics of free trade · Lack of updated norms · Inward-looking priorities · Divergent surplus and deficit nations. Say it: "The world SLID into statecraft." (own memory aid)

Disruptions during the pandemic

3 · NOWCASTING AND THE NATIONAL STATISTICAL SYSTEM (HANDOUT PAGES 13-19)
Understand it firstIf the speedometer is wrong, even a good driver gets it wrong. Section 3 is about fixing the dashboard: guessing the quarter's growth early (nowcasting), adding new surveys, and refreshing the base years of GDP, IIP, CPI and WPI. These pages are typed, so the content is kept in full below.
Nowcasting India's quarterly GDP growth
NoteDefinition: estimating the current quarter's GDP growth before official data is released, using high-frequency indicators.
HeadingHandout points
NeedReal-time growth assessment: in shocks like Covid-19 lockdowns activity changes fast, so direction must be estimated to guide policy. Overcome GDP data lag: official quarterly GDP comes after a delay, so early internal estimates guide timely policy.
AdvantagesProactive shock absorption (early detection of structural shifts or supply disruptions; useful in pandemic, war, oil-price rise, weak monsoon, financial instability, global slowdown) · Dynamic decision-making (data-driven, not only delayed official data or anecdotes) · Supports market expectations (investors, businesses, banks, rating agencies).
MethodThe RBI uses a Dynamic Factor Model (DFM), historically relying on 27 high-frequency indicators (HFIs) for industry, services and global activity. Of these, 17 HFIs are part of a specific nowcasting framework developed by the Government of India.
ChallengesData quality (errors, gaps, under-reporting, revisions) · informal-sector under-coverage · proxy limits (GST collections, e-way bills, electricity use, PMI only indirectly show growth) · short-term volatility (festivals, weather, base effects, policy changes, one-time events).
ConclusionNowcasting gives timely, evidence-based signals but should complement, not replace, official GDP estimates.
MNEMONICDIPSFour challenges of nowcasting: Data quality · Informal sector missed · Proxy indicators imperfect · Short-term volatility. Say it: "Nowcasts can DIP." (own memory aid)
New and changed surveys
New surveyWhat it is (handout)
ASISSE Annual Survey of Incorporated Service Sector EnterprisesNew NSO-MoSPI annual survey for the incorporated or organised service sector; State- and industry-level estimates of GVA, fixed capital, capital formation, employment, emoluments; uses GSTN-based datasets or frames.
AIDIS All India Debt and Investment SurveyNational survey of household debt, assets, liabilities and investment patterns. Next round planned for July 2026 to June 2027; these topics are kept out of the Household Income Survey because AIDIS covers them.
NHIS Household Income SurveyNew all-India survey on household income distribution and welfare, a long-standing gap; also sources and patterns of income and impact of technology on wages.
Existing surveyChange made
ASUSE (unincorporated enterprises)NIC 2025 replaces NIC 2008; CPC 3.0 (draft) for products; now released quarterly; new questions on logistics and operations.
PLFSFrom 2025: monthly and quarterly all-India estimates; sample design revamped, households per selected unit raised from 8 to 12, enabling district-level estimates; extra questions including education.
Forward-looking CAPEX SurveyExpected investments over two consecutive financial years; now a structured, web-based, forward-looking format capturing private investment intentions and actual capex.
Modular surveys (CMS)Short-duration Comprehensive Modular Surveys; under the NSS 80th Round separate modules on telecom and ICT skills and on education.
  • Modernising surveys: CAPI (Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing) with the cloud-based eSIGMA platform gives real-time validation, monitoring and geotagging; survey reports now come within 45 to 90 days, monthly results within 15 days.
GDP: base year 2011-12 → 2022-23
AreaProblem with the 2011-12 seriesSolution in the 2022-23 series
Base yearLost relevance as the economy changed (pandemic lockdowns, supply-chain shocks).A stable, post-pandemic anchor.
SectorsDid not fully capture new-age sectors such as digital services.Item basket updated to map digital services, intermediary platforms and green energy.
DataRelied on periodic manual surveys and broad proxy ratios: slow, blind spots.SQAF auditing and e-SIGMA; administrative footprints (like e-Vaahan) and high-frequency data (ASUSE, PLFS) make the informal economy visible; hired domestic workers included.
MethodSingle deflation (only total output adjusted for inflation); repeated gaps between production-side and expenditure-side estimates.Single extrapolation and double deflation (inputs and outputs adjusted separately); direct GST data; Supply and Use Tables (SUT) balance supply with demand, reducing statistical mismatches.
IIP: base year 2011-12 → 2022-23
AreaProblem with the 2011-12 seriesSolution in the 2022-23 series
Basket and coverageObsolete items (kerosene, CFLs); covered mainly mining, manufacturing, electricity.New items (electronic components, CCTV cameras) added; obsolete removed; adds Gas and Water Supply, Sewerage and Waste Management.
DataSample degradation (closed factories, non-response); no seasonal adjustment, so festivals and working days distorted short-term movements.Systematic selection and substitution of factories; electricity tracked separately as renewable and non-renewable; seasonal adjustment introduced.
MethodStatic, fixed indices; removal of "not elsewhere classified (n.e.c.)" items missed niche production.Chain-based indices (weights update dynamically); n.e.c. items reintroduced to capture new activities.
CPI: base year 2012 → 2024
AreaProblem with the 2012 seriesSolution in the 2024 series
BasketFood share 45.86%, declining in real spending; obsolete items (VCRs); headline too sensitive to food, too little to healthcare and education.Basket 299 → 358 items from HCES 2023-24; adds OTT subscriptions, rural house rent, CNG/PNG; food weight 45.86% → 36.75%.
DataPhysical market visits only; ignored e-commerce; struggled with merging rural-urban habits.CAPI on handheld devices; online prices tracked in large cities plus administrative data for flights and streaming; Housing Index rebuilt; linking factors and back series provided.
MethodOnly six broad groups buried rent and hospital bills; national baskets ignored state differences.COICOP-2018: 12 divisions (UN standard, globally comparable); state-specific baskets.
WPI: base year 2011-12 → 2022-23, then phased out for PPI
AreaProblem with the 2011-12 seriesSolution in the 2022-23 series
BasketOnly 697 items; poor representation of alternative energy.697 → 957 items; adds solar, wind and nuclear under electricity.
DataCrude petroleum and natural gas sat in Primary Articles; carry-forward method for missing prices caused stagnation.Crude petroleum and natural gas moved to Fuel and Power; Targeted Mean Imputation for missing prices.
MethodWeights by Net Traded Value distorted domestic production; static formulation.Weights by Gross Value of Output (GVO); chain-based elementary indices; strictly basic prices (excluding net taxes and trade or transport margins).
MNEMONICGIW 22-23 · C 24Base years in one line: GDP, IIP, WPI all move to 2022-23; CPI moves from 2012 to 2024. Say it: "Three twenty-two-twenty-threes and one twenty-four." (own memory aid)
Why WPI is being phased out by 2031 (four inherent weaknesses)
Total exclusion of services
Deflation distortions (a messy mix of WPI and CPI to deflate nominal GDP)
Global incompatibility (prices at the initial stage of transactions, against IMF practice)
Friction in business contracts (intermediate margins make it an inaccurate gauge of factory-gate pressure)
New Producer Price Index (released with the revised WPI)Significance
Output PPIProducer-level inflation from the output side: are producers getting higher or lower prices?
Input PPI (printed "Trial Input Producer Price Index")Input cost pressures: is inflation coming from rising production costs?
Service PPIBrings the services sector into producer-level inflation, which WPI largely misses.
Why PPI is better than WPI (six reasons)
1 · Better reflection of producer-level inflation
2 · Shows the input-output price relationship
3 · Tracks inflation pass-through
4 · Includes services
5 · Better for policy and national accounts (GDP deflators)
6 · Aligned with global practice (US, China, Japan, Germany, France, G-20)
NoteConclusion (handout): updated base years for GDP, CPI, IIP and WPI, and the move to PPI, make macro data more current, representative and globally comparable.
PYQ 2021 · 10m · GDP methodologyExplain the difference between computing methodology of India's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) before the year 2015 and after the year 2015.★ Write: Write the latest change from the handout: 2011-12 series used single deflation, proxy ratios and manual surveys; 2022-23 series uses double deflation, GST and administrative data (e-Vaahan, ASUSE, PLFS), SUT balancing, includes hired domestic workers and digital services.Where / gap: Section 3. Gap: the 2015 revision itself (change to 2011-12 base and corporate data) is not in this handout; add it from the textbook layer.
Short forms in section 3

AIDIS = All India Debt and Investment Survey (national survey of household debt, assets and investment)

ASISSE = Annual Survey of Incorporated Service Sector Enterprises (new NSO annual survey of organised services)

ASUSE = Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (survey of small unorganised enterprises, now quarterly)

CAPEX = Capital Expenditure (spending on assets; also the name of the forward-looking CAPEX Survey)

CAPI = Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (surveyors record answers on handheld devices with real-time checks)

CCTV = Closed-Circuit Television (camera surveillance used as a workplace safeguard for women on night shifts)

CMS = Comprehensive Modular Surveys (short surveys on a single policy topic)

CNG = Compressed Natural Gas (vehicle fuel now in the CPI basket)

COICOP = Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (UN standard that sorts household spending into 12 divisions)

CPC = Central Product Classification (standard code list for products)

CPI = Consumer Price Index (measures retail inflation from a basket of goods and services households buy)

DFM = Dynamic Factor Model (statistical model the RBI uses to nowcast GDP from many indicators)

GDP = Gross Domestic Product (value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year)

GST = Goods and Services Tax (India's indirect tax on goods and services)

GVA = Gross Value Added (value of output minus inputs, by sector; the supply side of GDP)

GVO = Gross Value of Output (total value of what is produced; the new WPI weighting basis)

HCES = Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (survey of what households spend; used for the CPI basket)

HFIs = High-Frequency Indicators (data released often (monthly, weekly) such as GST, e-way bills, power use)

ICT = Information and Communication Technology (computers, internet and digital tools; taught as an employability skill)

IIP = Index of Industrial Production (monthly index of output in mining, manufacturing and electricity)

IMF = International Monetary Fund (global body whose statistical standards PPI follows)

MoSPI = Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (ministry that publishes national statistics)

NHIS = National Household Income Survey (new survey on household income distribution and welfare)

NIC = National Industrial Classification (standard code list for industries; 2025 version replaces 2008)

NSO = National Statistics Office (part of MoSPI; runs PLFS)

NSS = National Sample Survey (earlier survey regions that PLFS replaced with districts)

OTT = Over-The-Top (streaming services delivered over the internet)

PLFS = Periodic Labour Force Survey (NSO survey that measures employment and unemployment (LFPR, WPR, UR))

PMI = Purchasing Managers' Index (survey index of business activity; used as a growth proxy)

PNG = Piped Natural Gas (household cooking gas now in the CPI basket)

PPI = Producer Price Index (index of prices producers receive for goods and services; replaces WPI)

RBI = Reserve Bank of India (India's central bank)

SQAF = Statistical Quality Assessment Framework (audit framework for data quality)

SUT = Supply and Use Tables (tables that balance total supply of goods with their uses to cut statistical mismatches)

UN = United Nations (international body whose COICOP standard CPI follows)

US = United States (the USA)

WPI = Wholesale Price Index (index of goods prices at the wholesale stage; being phased out for PPI)

4 · MEDIUM-TERM GROWTH POTENTIAL (HANDOUT PAGES 19-20)
Understand it firstPotential growth is the speed the economy can keep up without overheating. The question the handout asks: "Has high GDP growth and low inflation left the Indian economy in a good state?" The answer: the base is stronger (potential near 7%), but there are frictions, so the right attitude is caution, not pessimism.
The positives
Upward shift in potential growth
The 7% milestone: reforms have lifted medium-term potential growth closer to 7 per cent
A higher growth ceiling: productive capacity strengthened; ceiling shifted upward
Sustained momentum: growth stays above pre-pandemic averages: no reversion to the old sluggish trend
Three structural drivers of potential growth
Capital stock growth: investment revival and capacity expansion
Sustained public capex: less logistics bottleneck
Productivity boosters: physical infrastructure supported by digital systems and reforms
Crowding-in of private investment with healthier corporate and bank balance sheets
Labour input: participation, formalisation, employability
Rising participation, especially of women, with wider social-security cover
Lower market frictions (deregulation, trust-based compliance)
Workforce quality (education, health, skilling, apprenticeships)
Formalisation transition after the pandemic shocks
Trend TFP: productivity and efficiency gains
Digital catalyst: DPI lowers transaction cost and leakages
Allocative efficiency: easier firm entry and exit
Lower cost of scaling: roads, airports, logistics, simpler regulation
MNEMONICTLCThree drivers of potential growth: TFP (trend productivity) · Labour input · Capital stock. Say it: "Growth needs TLC." (own memory aid; order of the handout is capital, labour, TFP)
PYQ 2020 · 10m · Potential GDPDefine potential GDP and explain its determinants. What are the factors that have been inhibiting India from realizing its potential GDP?★ Write: Define: medium-term growth the economy can sustain (handout: potential closer to 7%). Determinants: capital stock (public capex, private investment), labour input (participation, formalisation, skills), trend TFP (DPI, allocative efficiency, lower cost of scaling). Inhibitors: the five frictions (nominal growth about 8%, jobs mismatch worsened by AI, private investment hesitation, external pressure, strategic gap).Where / gap: Section 4. Gap: the handout gives no formal definition of potential GDP; use the textbook layer.
PYQ 2017 · 10m · Potential growthAmong several factors for India's potential growth, savings rate is the most effective one. Do you agree? What are the other factors available for growth potential?★ Write: Other factors from the handout: capital stock (public capex, private investment crowding-in), labour input (women's participation, skilling, formalisation), trend TFP (digital public infrastructure, easier entry and exit, lower scaling cost).Where / gap: Section 4. Gap: the handout does not discuss the savings rate; add that part from the textbook layer.
The other side: macroeconomic frictions
Five frictions (caution, not pessimism)
Growth-demand constraint: nominal growth in single digits (about 8%) limits tax buoyancy, fiscal space and debt management; very subdued core inflation (about 2%) may also signal weak consumer demand
Employment-productivity mismatch: joblessness high, especially among graduates; deeper problem is education-to-job mismatch, now intensified by AI-led disruption of cognitive and service work
Private investment hesitation: not fully revived despite supply-side incentives and public capex
External sector pressure: a goods trade deficit and dependence on foreign capital inflows; when inflows weaken the rupee comes under pressure
Strategic and global risk: the Lowy Institute's Power Gap Index scores India at -4.0 (operating below its strategic potential in Asia); financial, technological and geopolitical stresses can combine
MNEMONICNEPALFive frictions: Nominal growth slow (about 8%) · Employment mismatch · Private investment shy · Account (external) pressure on the rupee · Lowy power gap (-4.0). Say it: "Growth hits a NEPAL-sized hill." (own memory aid)
The way forward: resilience and indispensability
Building resilience and indispensability (five steps)
Resilience first: resource buffers, secure supply chains, diversify payment systems
Entrepreneurial state: trust-based deregulation, faster decisions, room to take risks and scale
Strategic indispensability: make Indian goods, services and capabilities hard to replace
Private-sector responsibility: face competition, invest at scale, be globally competitive, not only domestically comfortable
Long-term resilience: durable capacity, Centre-State coordination, innovation and institutional reform towards Viksit Bharat
MNEMONICRESPLFive way-forward steps: Resilience first · Entrepreneurial state · Strategic indispensability · Private-sector responsibility · Long-term resilience. Read it "re-spell": "Respell India's growth story." (own memory aid, handout order)
NoteConclusion (handout): a volatile world demands caution, but India's strong macro fundamentals leave no room for pessimism; prioritise strategic resilience and continuous innovation over short-term fixes to stay the course to Viksit Bharat.
Short forms in section 4

AI = Artificial Intelligence (computer systems that do tasks needing human-like learning or judgement)

DPI = Digital Public Infrastructure (shared digital systems (ID, payments, data) that many services can build on)

GDP = Gross Domestic Product (value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year)

TFP = Total Factor Productivity (output growth not explained by more capital or labour: efficiency and technology)

ABBREVIATION COLUMN
Abbreviation columnEvery short form in this chapter, with its full form and a one-line plain meaning. The meanings are plain-language aids to help revision: verify them before quoting in an answer.

AEs: Advanced Economies. rich countries such as the US, UK, Japan, euro area

AI: Artificial Intelligence. computer systems that do tasks needing human-like learning or judgement

AIDIS: All India Debt and Investment Survey. national survey of household debt, assets and investment

ASISSE: Annual Survey of Incorporated Service Sector Enterprises. new NSO annual survey of organised services

ASUSE: Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises. survey of small unorganised enterprises, now quarterly

BE: Budget Estimate. the figure planned in the Budget

CAPEX: Capital Expenditure. spending on assets; also the name of the forward-looking CAPEX Survey

CAPI: Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing. surveyors record answers on handheld devices with real-time checks

CBAM: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. EU charge on imports like steel and cement based on their embedded emissions

CCTV: Closed-Circuit Television. camera surveillance used as a workplace safeguard for women on night shifts

CMS: Comprehensive Modular Surveys. short surveys on a single policy topic

CNG: Compressed Natural Gas. vehicle fuel now in the CPI basket

COICOP: Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose. UN standard that sorts household spending into 12 divisions

CPC: Central Product Classification. standard code list for products

CPI: Consumer Price Index. measures retail inflation from a basket of goods and services households buy

DFM: Dynamic Factor Model. statistical model the RBI uses to nowcast GDP from many indicators

DPI: Digital Public Infrastructure. shared digital systems (ID, payments, data) that many services can build on

EMDEs: Emerging Market and Developing Economies. countries such as India, China, Mexico, Indonesia

EU: European Union. the bloc of European countries

EVs: Electric Vehicles. vehicles run on batteries; a strategic sector

FAE: First Advance Estimate. first official estimate of annual GDP, made before the year ends

FDI: Foreign Direct Investment. long-term investment by a foreign firm in a business in another country

FPI: Foreign Portfolio Investment. foreign money invested in shares and bonds; flows in and out quickly

FY23: Financial Year 2022-23. April 2022 to March 2023

FY25: Financial Year 2024-25. April 2024 to March 2025

FY26: Financial Year 2025-26. April 2025 to March 2026

GDP: Gross Domestic Product. value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year

GER: Gross Enrolment Ratio. students enrolled as a share of the age group meant for that level

GFCE: Government Final Consumption Expenditure. government spending on its own consumption; part of GDP

GFCF: Gross Fixed Capital Formation. investment in assets like machinery, buildings and infrastructure; the investment part of GDP

GNPA: Gross Non-Performing Assets. total bad loans of banks as a share of loans (the handout gives 2.2%)

GST: Goods and Services Tax. India's indirect tax on goods and services

GVA: Gross Value Added. value of output minus inputs, by sector; the supply side of GDP

GVO: Gross Value of Output. total value of what is produced; the new WPI weighting basis

HCES: Household Consumption Expenditure Survey. survey of what households spend; used for the CPI basket

HFIs: High-Frequency Indicators. data released often (monthly, weekly) such as GST, e-way bills, power use

ICT: Information and Communication Technology. computers, internet and digital tools; taught as an employability skill

IIP: Index of Industrial Production. monthly index of output in mining, manufacturing and electricity

IMF: International Monetary Fund. global body whose statistical standards PPI follows

IMR: Infant Mortality Rate. infant deaths per 1,000 live births

IT: Information Technology. software and computer-based services

MoSPI: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. ministry that publishes national statistics

NABARD: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development. apex rural finance bank; runs a rural economic sentiments survey

NHIS: National Household Income Survey. new survey on household income distribution and welfare

NIC: National Industrial Classification. standard code list for industries; 2025 version replaces 2008

NPA: Non-Performing Asset. a bank loan that has stopped being repaid

NSO: National Statistics Office. part of MoSPI; runs PLFS

NSS: National Sample Survey. earlier survey regions that PLFS replaced with districts

OTT: Over-The-Top. streaming services delivered over the internet

PFCE: Private Final Consumption Expenditure. household spending; the consumption part of GDP

PLFS: Periodic Labour Force Survey. NSO survey that measures employment and unemployment (LFPR, WPR, UR)

PMI: Purchasing Managers' Index. survey index of business activity; used as a growth proxy

PNG: Piped Natural Gas. household cooking gas now in the CPI basket

PPI: Producer Price Index. index of prices producers receive for goods and services; replaces WPI

RBI: Reserve Bank of India. India's central bank

RE: Revised Estimate. the updated figure for the running year

SQAF: Statistical Quality Assessment Framework. audit framework for data quality

SUT: Supply and Use Tables. tables that balance total supply of goods with their uses to cut statistical mismatches

TFP: Total Factor Productivity. output growth not explained by more capital or labour: efficiency and technology

UK: United Kingdom. Britain

UN: United Nations. international body whose COICOP standard CPI follows

UNCTAD: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development. UN body that publishes the World Investment Report

US: United States. the USA

USA: United States of America. one of the countries the handout names for school-level vocational exposure

USD: United States Dollar. currency used to state external figures

WALR: Weighted Average Lending Rate. average interest rate banks charge on loans

WPI: Wholesale Price Index. index of goods prices at the wholesale stage; being phased out for PPI
